title: Which voice surprised you
hookLine: a tradition you didn't expect to learn from
last: WHICH ONE IS QUIETLY CARRYING YOU.

lines: A LOT OF VOICES IN ONE ROOM.
cards: A Stoic emperor on grief. A Sufi poet on love. A Zen saying about chopping wood.

A psalm about still waters. A Sikh hymn, a Jewish blessing, a Hindu warrior on a battlefield, a Christian cook at a kitchen stove. This year put a lot of voices in one room, not all of them ones you expected.
Maybe one of them stopped you: a line you didn't see coming, from a place you didn't expect to learn anything from.

teach.b: First, a scene from the book of Acts. Paul, the Christian apostle, stands in Athens before a crowd of Greek philosophers.
He's there to speak about the God of Israel and about Jesus, and in the middle of it he quotes their own poets back to them.
In the King James words: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring."
He found a line worth repeating in someone else's tradition, and he named where it came from. Second, why naming matters. Paul didn't pretend the line was his.
He said: your poets said this.

teach.h: MARCUS THANKS EACH TEACHER BY NAME.
teach.b: That's a small act of honesty, and also a kind of thanks. It's the rule this path has kept all year: every teaching keeps its own name on it, and no voice is folded into another. Third, a man who thanked people by name.
Marcus Aurelius opened his private notebook, known as the Meditations, with a list. From his grandfather he learned good character and an even temper. From his mother, generosity and simple living.
From a teacher, to bear hardship and want little. On it goes, person after person, each with one thing learned. He never ranked them.
A voice you expected can confirm what you already know. One you didn't expect can stretch you. It doesn't mean leaving where you stand, or changing who you are.
It means someone from another room handed you something, and it fit.

how: People on a spiritual path of their own sometimes read across traditions and keep each teaching's source attached; some keep a list of teachers and lines they're grateful for, as Marcus Aurelius did in the first book of the Meditations.

games.q: you're Paul, speaking to Greek philosophers in Athens. you know a line from their own poets that fits what you want to say. what do you do?
o: use it, and say it's your own idea.
quote it, and name it as theirs.
avoid it: it comes from outside your tradition.
games.why: "as certain also of your own poets have said": Paul quotes the line and names where it came from.

practice: Let this year's voices pass by in your mind, and wait for the one that tugs a little, the line that surprised you.

Name it, out loud or silently: the line, whose it was and where it came from, the way Paul named the poets and Marcus his teachers. Then thank it, in your own prayer if you pray, or with a plain thank you if you don't.

wordCard.voice: Marcus Aurelius. He named his teachers one by one in his notebook, the way Paul named the poets who surprised him from another room. Today's word.
